smallTalk: The harvest was good this year, thanks be to the gods.
The roads are safe, as long as you travel by day.
The new temple is finished, and they are already planning a bigger one.
The king's messengers ride faster every year.
Everyone says the empire will last forever. Everyone always says that.
The harbour has more foreign ships than local ones these days.
The bells rang all week for the feast.
Taxes again. Always taxes.
Riders came through with news from the far side of the world.
The roads belong to whoever holds the next castle.
Every week a new pamphlet, every month a new war.
The post rides faster than ever.
Every scholar in town owns a new instrument and argues about it.
The printers cannot keep up with the quarrels.
The smoke never lifts over the mills.
Everyone talks about the railway.
Concerts every night, and revolutions every other week.
The coffee houses are louder than the courts.
The newspapers are banned on Monday and back on Tuesday.
Everyone is writing a manifesto. Even the baker.
The news never stops, day or night.
Everything is on the radio now.
The maglev was late again. Some things never change.
Everyone at home says the timeline feels different lately.

places.moment: Thebes during the reign of Hatshepsut, c. 1470 BCE (her architect Senenmut; 'scribes of the fields' re-measuring land with knotted ropes after each Nile flood)
smallTalk: The Nile rose right on time; the fields are black and rich.

places.moment: Mamluk Cairo under al-Nasir Muhammad, c. 1340 CE (the al-Khalij al-Nasiri canal was dug in 1325 and the Nile flood was read at the Roda Nilometer)
Ottoman Cairo, c. 1700 (Cairo as hub of the Red Sea coffee trade; the yearly cutting of the Khalij canal dam at the Nile flood)
Cairo in 1869, the year Khedive Isma'il opened the Suez Canal, during the building of the new irrigation canal network
Egypt under Gamal Abdel Nasser, Cairo and Aswan, c. 1962 (Aswan High Dam under construction 1960-70; Suez Canal nationalised 1956)
Pi-Ramesses in the Nile Delta under Ramesses II, c. 1250 BCE (the new capital of chariot workshops, the temples of Abu Simbel and the first written peace treaty, with the Hittites)
smallTalk: The new capital in the Delta smells of fresh paint and horses.

places.moment: Alexandria under Cleopatra VII, c. 45 BCE (the Library and the Museum, the Pharos lighthouse and a harbour full of Roman grain ships)
smallTalk: The Library lent me a scroll. I am told I must return it this century.

places.moment: Cairo under Saladin, c. 1187, the year he takes Jerusalem: the new Citadel on the Muqattam hill and the long city walls
smallTalk: They are cutting a well into the rock under the new Citadel. It goes down forever.

places.moment: Babylon under Hammurabi, c. 1760 BCE (the law code, clay contracts sealed with cylinder seals)
smallTalk: The scribes are busy; every jar of barley gets its tablet.

places.moment: Baghdad under the Abbasids, c. 830 CE (al-Khwarizmi at the House of Wisdom; translation and algebra)
Baghdad under the governor Hasan Pasha (1704-1723), whose household grew into the Mamluk regime, c. 1720 (notaries recording contracts for the qadi court registers)
Baghdad under the reforming governor Midhat Pasha, c. 1870 (Iraq's first printing press and first newspaper, al-Zawra, 1869)
Baghdad c. 1956, the Development Board's modernist building boom (commissions for Gropius, Le Corbusier and Wright) in the city where Zaha Hadid grew up
Athens in the age of Pericles and Socrates, c. 430 BCE
smallTalk: Everyone argues in the agora, and nobody agrees.

places.moment: Mystras, capital of the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, in the circle of the philosopher Gemistos Plethon, c. 1430
Greek Orthodox merchant community of Ioannina (Epirus) under Ottoman rule, c. 1700
Athens, new capital of the independent Greek kingdom, c. 1860
Athens after the fall of the junta and the restoration of democracy, c. 1975
Pella, capital of Macedon, in 336 BCE, as Philip II dies and his son Alexander takes the throne; Aristotle has tutored him at Mieza
smallTalk: The young king wants to march east. Everyone else wants to go home.

places.moment: Rome in the last years of the Republic, under Julius Caesar, c. 50 BCE
smallTalk: The Senate talks, the legions march.

places.moment: Florence of the Medici bank, during the Council of Florence, 1439
Milan under Ludovico Sforza, while Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper and designed machines, c. 1495
Bologna and Pontecchio, where young Guglielmo Marconi ran his first radio experiments, 1895
Rome during the economic miracle, the year of 'La Dolce Vita', 1960
Syracuse in Sicily under King Hiero II, c. 230 BCE, where Archimedes builds war machines and works out the lever, the screw and the volume of a crown
smallTalk: The old man by the harbour keeps shouting in the bath. Nobody minds any more.

places.moment: Venice in 1295, as Marco Polo comes home from twenty-four years at the court of Kublai Khan with paper money in his pockets and stories nobody believes
smallTalk: Some merchant came home saying coins are made of paper. The whole Rialto laughed.

places.moment: Padua and Venice in 1610, when Galileo turns his telescope on the sky, finds four moons around Jupiter and publishes the Starry Messenger
smallTalk: The professor sold the Senate a spyglass. Now everyone looks up instead of down.

places.moment: Luoyang, the Eastern Han capital, c. 105 CE, when Cai Lun presented his improved paper to the court
Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital, c. 1075. This is the era of Shen Kuo, scholar-official and envoy to the Liao, and of the magnetic compass and movable type.
Suzhou and Jiangnan in the late Ming, c. 1635, during the printing and publishing boom that produced Song Yingxing's illustrated technology encyclopedia Tiangong Kaiwu (1637)
Shanghai in the late Qing, c. 1880: the Shenbao newspaper, the Jiangnan Arsenal translation bureau and the first telegraph lines
Beijing, c. 1972, when Tu Youyou's Project 523 team isolated artemisinin at the Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Qufu, capital of the state of Lu, c. 500 BCE, in the Spring and Autumn period, while Confucius teaches the rites and generals across the states write on the art of war
smallTalk: Everyone in Qufu has an opinion on the proper bow.

places.moment: Xianyang, capital of the first emperor, c. 215 BCE: one script, one coin, one standard axle width, the terracotta army and the first great walls
smallTalk: They have standardised the cart axles. Next, they say, the jokes.

places.moment: Zhongdu, the Jin capital where Beijing stands, in 1215, the year Genghis Khan's riders take it; the Mongol relay posts reach across Asia
smallTalk: A rider passed through with a message from three thousand miles away. He was not even tired.

places.moment: Yamato (the Nara–Osaka plain) in the Kofun period, c. 450 CE, the age of the great keyhole tombs and haniwa clay figures
Kyoto under the Ashikaga shogunate, c. 1400: Kitayama culture, Noh theatre, and Japanese folding fans exported to Ming China
Edo and Sunpu at the founding of the Tokugawa shogunate, c. 1610, in Tokugawa Ieyasu's time. He received a Spanish mechanical clock in 1611.
Nagoya in the Meiji period, c. 1899, the time of Sakichi Toyoda's steam-powered wooden loom (1896) and Japan's rapid industrialisation
Tokyo during the Walkman boom, c. 1980, as Akio Morita's Sony took Japanese electronics global
Azuchi on Lake Biwa, c. 1576, where Oda Nobunaga raises the first great castle keep and frees the markets in the middle of a hundred years of war
smallTalk: The lord has opened the markets to anyone. Even the monks are selling.

places.moment: Edo, c. 1830, the floating world at its height: Kabuki, cheap woodblock prints sold in the street and a great wave about to be printed
smallTalk: A painter keeps changing his name. He is on his thirtieth.

places.moment: Camulodunum (Colchester), the trading capital of the Catuvellauni under Cunobelinus, c. 20 CE: shortly before the Roman conquest, while wine and luxury goods were arriving from Roman Gaul
London under Edward the Confessor, c. 1050: a North Sea port trading wool and silver, where laws of the time mention merchants from Flanders, Normandy and the German Empire
The Royal Exchange in London, c. 1600, the year the East India Company received its charter
London in 1843, when Ada Lovelace published her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, as the Cooke-Wheatstone electric telegraph spread and just before Railway Mania (1845-47)
Manchester, c. 1950, where Alan Turing was working on the university's pioneering stored-program computer (the Manchester Mark 1, built commercially by Ferranti)
London in 1687, rebuilt in brick after the Great Fire: the Royal Society, the coffee houses and Newton's Principia, the year it is printed
smallTalk: Apples fall in London just as in Lincolnshire. A man wrote a book about it.

places.moment: Free Germania east of the Rhine and north of the Danube, c. 98 CE, as described in Tacitus' Germania
The Rhine cities of Strasbourg and Mainz, c. 1440, when Johannes Gutenberg was running his first experiments with movable metal type

Nuremberg c. 1525: Duerer's city and Europe's hub of printing and precision instruments (Henlein's early portable spring-driven clocks, Behaim's globe), the year the city council adopted the Reformation as Luther's printed pamphlets spread
Berlin c. 1899, during the boom in German electrical engineering (Siemens, AEG) and chemistry (Bayer's aspirin, synthetic dyes), when Berlin's permanent dress-reform exhibition opened
Berlin c. 1926, the Weimar Republic's golden age of science and design: Einstein directs the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics, and the Bauhaus has just moved to Dessau
Bonn, seat of the Elector of Cologne, in 1790, where the young court organist Ludwig van Beethoven is about to leave for Vienna to study with Haydn
smallTalk: The organist's boy plays so loud the chandeliers shake. He says that is the point.

places.moment: Cologne in 1848, the year of revolutions: barricades in the German cities, the Communist Manifesto just printed and Karl Marx editing the Neue Rheinische Zeitung
smallTalk: The paper was banned again this morning. It will be on sale again by noon.

NEW: the Departure Manifest. Its Citizen ID, transponder and class must match the Citizen Account. The visa's photo must be the person at the desk (Look > Their face).
NEW: closed destinations. Refuse anyone bound for a place today's Directive Memo closes. Every paper's seal must match its office's in the Seal Register, now on your shelf.
NEW: the Stranding Waiver. A Standard visa rides an Economy transponder with a signed waiver; a Premium visa rides a Premium one.
NEW: the proof of means. A Standard visa also needs a Holiday Credit Agreement, a Proof of Funds or Travel Insurance.
NEW: the displaced. Their Displacement Certificate must match the Displacement Registry before they go home.
NEW: dress for the destination. A garment from another time or place causes a panic: check the Costume Guide.
NEW: Debt Relief labourers. A registered Labour Contract, an Economy transponder and a signed Stranding Waiver.
NEW: debt standing. Citizens in debt depart only on Debt Relief, and a Frozen account may not depart at all.
NEW: transponder recall. Every Driftbox 3 unit is grounded: refuse any departure on one.

Only after I read clause 9. There is no clause 9. Come back when there is.

{value}! Definitely {value}! Isn't it a lovely day?

{other}. Obviously. It always is.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: News? Only a rumour: someone sells pocket calculators to the ancients.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: They say a courier from your own century carries them. Watch for anyone who counts too fast.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Calculators? I saw nothing. Nothing at all.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: My temple at Abu Simbel has four of me out front. Each one larger than the last.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: We signed the first peace treaty ever written. They still say they won Kadesh. They did not.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Periclean Athens! My honeymoon. Well, our honeymoon. Dmitri's account froze on Tuesday.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: The brochure says the owls are real. Dmitri can have the postcard. I read every form, you know.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Me again! New waiver, signed in blue, like the lady said. Third line from the bottom.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: My Driftbox! It beeps when it's happy. It beeps a lot. Is that a lot?

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Me again! New unit, signed waiver, proof of means. What's this notice about a range limit?

choices.label: Economy units can't reach Athens now.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Then I'll save for a Premium. Tell the owls to wait for me. Tell Dmitri... actually, don't.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Desk 4 closed this morning. The Drive found my account on Tuesday, and the Drive doesn't wait.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: They're sending it to you. Sorry. Keep the good pen, it's in the second drawer.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Luck is a Premium feature. I'm on Economy.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: My business in Strasbourg? Mirrors. Pilgrims buy little mirrors to catch the holy light.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Mirrors. And a small press. A very small press. Please do not write that down.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Best contract in the building, this. Read it twice if you like. I'll wait.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Of course. And for a clerk who reads quickly, there's 200 cr in it. Between friends.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Pleasure doing business.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Suit yourself. It was a very quick 200.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: The Analytical Engine will weave algebra as the loom weaves flowers. I wrote that, you know.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: In 1843, of course. Where else would I have been? Is that a trick question?

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: It froze on Tuesday. The Drive put me on its list on Monday. You see my problem.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: My father's waiver passed his debt to me when he didn't come back. The colliery was my way out.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Nobody can. Stamp it quickly, then. Everyone else does.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Routine leisure departure. Republican Rome. I hear the concrete is excellent.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Only my patience. Take all the time the Directorate pays you for. I'll be timing it.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Routine leisure departure. Republican Rome. The Tyburn Mills sent us a very interesting contract.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Stamped here, on day eleven. Two hundred credits went missing the same day. Curious, isn't it?

premades.name: Cleopatra
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt. Her barge is double-parked.
premades.recordNote: Queen of Egypt, last of the Ptolemies. Speaks nine languages. Rome owes her a great deal of grain.

premades.name: Ramesses II
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Ramesses II, Pharaoh of Egypt. He would like a bigger desk.
premades.recordNote: Pharaoh of Egypt, builder of Abu Simbel. Signed the first written peace treaty. Has over a hundred children.

premades.name: Saladin
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Saladin, Sultan of Egypt and Syria. He is famously polite.
premades.recordNote: Sultan of Egypt and Syria. Retook Jerusalem. Known for mercy to his enemies and for giving his treasury away.

premades.name: Umm Kulthum
premades.recordNote: Singer of Cairo. Her Thursday concerts empty the streets.

premades.name: Hammurabi
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Hammurabi, King of Babylon. He has brought his own laws.
premades.recordNote: King of Babylon and lawgiver. Travels with a stone slab of 282 laws.

premades.name: Muhammad al-Khwarizmi
premades.recordNote: Scholar of the House of Wisdom. Writes on calculation.

premades.name: Alexander the Great
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Alexander the Great, King of Macedon. He is twenty and in a hurry.
premades.recordNote: King of Macedon, twenty. Taught by Aristotle. Intends to march to the end of the world, possibly by Tuesday.

premades.name: Aristotle
premades.recordNote: Philosopher and tutor to the prince of Macedon. Has written on everything, including queues, probably.

premades.name: Socrates
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Socrates of Athens. He asks more questions than you do.
premades.recordNote: Philosopher. Known to question officials at length.

premades.name: Archimedes
premades.recordNote: Mathematician and engineer of Syracuse. Shouts in baths. Can move the Earth, given a place to stand.

premades.name: Julius Caesar
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Gaius Julius Caesar. He came, he saw, he queued.
premades.recordNote: General and Dictator of Rome. Crossed the Rubicon. In debt to half the Senate. Avoid the Ides of March.

premades.name: Marco Polo
premades.recordNote: Merchant of Venice, back from twenty-four years at Kublai Khan's court. Nobody believes his stories.

premades.name: Galileo Galilei
premades.recordNote: Professor of mathematics at Padua. Has seen four moons around Jupiter. Argues with everyone about it.

premades.name: Leonardo da Vinci
premades.recordNote: Painter and engineer in the service of the Duke of Milan.

premades.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
premades.recordNote: Sculptor of Florence, twenty. Looking for a good block of marble. Dislikes painting.

premades.name: Confucius
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Master Kong, called Confucius. He bows exactly the right amount.
premades.recordNote: Teacher of Lu. Believes in proper conduct, proper rites and proper forms. Approves of your desk, cautiously.

premades.name: Qin Shi Huang
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Qin Shi Huang, First Emperor of China. He has standardised the queue.
premades.recordNote: First Emperor of a united China. Standardised the script, the coin and the axles. Searching for an elixir of life.

premades.name: Sun Tzu
premades.recordNote: General and author of The Art of War. Wins most battles without fighting. Treats the queue as terrain.

premades.name: Genghis Khan
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Genghis Khan, Great Khan of the Mongols. His horse is in the queue too.
premades.recordNote: Great Khan of the Mongols. Rules from the Pacific to the Caspian. Runs a postal relay faster than anything alive.

premades.name: Oda Nobunaga
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Oda Nobunaga, lord of Azuchi. He is building the biggest castle in Japan.
premades.recordNote: Warlord of Owari and Azuchi. Unifying Japan by force. Freed the markets. Wears a European cape on special days.

premades.name: Katsushika Hokusai
premades.recordNote: Painter of Edo, seventy. Has moved house ninety times and changed his name thirty. Working on a big wave.

premades.name: Akira Kurosawa
premades.recordNote: Film director of Tokyo. Shooting a war epic in colour. Wears dark glasses indoors.

premades.name: Elizabeth I
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth I. Do not mention marriage.
premades.recordNote: Queen of England and Ireland. Defeated the Armada. Signed the East India Company's charter this year.

premades.name: Isaac Newton
premades.recordNote: Lucasian Professor of Mathematics. Wrote the laws of motion and gravity. Later Master of the Royal Mint.

premades.name: William Shakespeare
premades.recordNote: Playwright of London. Part-owner of the Globe. Borrows his plots and admits it.

premades.name: Ada Lovelace
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Ada Lovelace, of London.
premades.recordNote: Mathematician, of London. Registered on arrival, in her own hand.

premades.name: Charles Darwin
premades.recordNote: Naturalist of Kent. Back from a long voyage. Keeps beetles in his pockets.

premades.name: Alan Turing
premades.recordNote: Mathematician at Manchester. Asks whether machines can think.

premades.name: Johannes Gutenberg
premades.recordNote: Goldsmith of Mainz. Business in Strasbourg undisclosed.

premades.name: Martin Luther
premades.recordNote: Monk and professor of Wittenberg. Nailed 95 theses to a door. Translated the Bible into German for everyone.

premades.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
premades.recordNote: Court organist of Bonn, nineteen. Leaving for Vienna to study with Haydn. Plays everything very loudly.

premades.name: Karl Marx
premades.recordNote: Journalist and philosopher of Trier. Co-wrote the Communist Manifesto. Editing a newspaper that keeps being banned.

premades.name: Albert Einstein
premades.intro: Priority arrival: Albert Einstein. He says your clock is wrong. Relatively.
premades.recordNote: Physicist of Berlin. Thinks about light and clocks. Has patented a refrigerator.

premades.name: Pell Quimby
premades.recordNote: Honeymoon departure. Travelling alone.

premades.name: Ines Varga
premades.intro: Next! Step forward... Ines? From Desk 4?
premades.recordNote: Temporal Customs, Desk 4. Debt Relief departure booked.

premades.name: Rook Danner
premades.recordNote: No remarks on file.

premades.name: Marek Hollis
premades.recordNote: Debt passed from kin, 2147.

premades.name: Quill Ferreira
premades.recordNote: No remarks on file.

rules.name: Hieroglyphs in Babylon

rules.name: Ines at the mills

rules.name: Ines rebooked
rules.news: Ines Varga's Debt Relief departure was refused at Desk 3. Collections have rebooked her.

rules.name: The rift storm
rules.news: RIFT STORM: hundreds were pulled out of their own time overnight. The intake halls are full.

rules.name: Gutenberg's press
rules.news: THE PRESS ROLLS: Johannes Gutenberg, stamped home at Desk 3, prints with movable metal type in Mainz. Every Rhine city reads.

rules.name: The Driftbox recall
rules.news: RECALL: a Driftbox 3 tour group is lost in Babylonia. Every Driftbox 3 is grounded from today.

rules.name: Rook's contract
rules.news: The Tyburn Mills report a new hand with a very interesting contract.

rules.name: Rook's complaint
rules.news: COMPLAINT: a labourer refused at Desk 3 says the clerk pocketed his 200 cr first. The Directorate has opened a file.

rules.name: A lady with a glowing wrist
rules.news: A LADY WITH A GLOWING WRIST: the "Ada Lovelace" stamped through at Desk 3 shows London a 2150 wrist comm. Society is intrigued.

rules.name: The Lovelace enthusiast
rules.news: The 'Ada Lovelace' refused at Desk 3 was a 2150 enthusiast. She has been sent home with a caution.

rules.name: Audit week
rules.news: DIRECTORATE: auditors will test the desks this week. Any traveller may be one.

rules.name: The range limit
rules.news: RANGE LIMIT: after Babylonia, cheap Economy units no longer reach the Ancient era. From today, no Economy traveller goes there.

rules.name: A frozen account departs
rules.news: A frozen account left on Debt Relief from Desk 3. Collections have questions.

rules.name: Collections call
rules.news: Collections called at a Hollis address last night. Nobody answered.

rules.name: The audit passed
rules.news: AUDIT: Desk 3 caught the Directorate's test traveller. A commendation goes on file.

rules.name: The audit failed
rules.news: AUDIT: Desk 3 approved the Directorate's test traveller. It goes on file.

rules.name: The audit finds the two hundred
rules.news: AUDIT: a forged Labour Contract passed Desk 3 on day 11, with 200 cr beside it. It goes on file.

rules.name: The Drive's last day
rules.news: The Drive's last day. Premium families book the summer; Debt Relief books everyone else.

rules.name: Umm Kulthum sings at home
rules.news: THURSDAY NIGHT: Umm Kulthum, stamped home at Desk 3, sings Cairo a song about 2150. The streets empty to listen.

rules.name: Al-Khwarizmi's algorithm
rules.news: THE ALGORITHM: al-Khwarizmi, stamped home at Desk 3, teaches the House of Wisdom 2150's arithmetic. Baghdad computes.

rules.name: "Socrates" in the agora
rules.news: QUESTIONS IN ATHENS: the "Socrates" stamped through at Desk 3 asks the agora about 2150. Nobody has an answer yet.

rules.name: Leonardo's flying machine
rules.news: IT FLIES: Leonardo da Vinci, stamped home at Desk 3, finishes his flying machine from 2150's sketches. Milan takes off.

rules.name: Turing's thinking machine
rules.news: THINKING MACHINES: Alan Turing, stamped home at Desk 3, builds 2150's computer in Manchester. It answers back.

rules.name: Ramesses builds bigger
rules.news: COLOSSAL: Ramesses II, stamped home at Desk 3, builds a temple to 2150 at Abu Simbel. It has four of him out front.

rules.name: Cleopatra's Alexandria
rules.news: THE QUEEN COMES HOME: Cleopatra, stamped home at Desk 3, opens 2150's library in Alexandria. Rome asks for a card.

rules.name: Saladin's open treasury
rules.news: THE GENEROUS SULTAN: Saladin, stamped home at Desk 3, gives Cairo's treasury to 2150's poor. He dies with one coin.

rules.name: Alexander pays every debt
rules.news: ALL DEBTS PAID: Alexander the Great, stamped home at Desk 3, pays his whole army's debts with 2150's credit. Macedon owes nothing.

rules.name: Aristotle classifies 2150
rules.news: EVERYTHING HAS A CATEGORY: Aristotle, stamped home at Desk 3, files 2150 under Logic. Every scholar in Greece adopts the system.

rules.name: Confucius' examinations
rules.news: THE PROPER FORM: Confucius, stamped home at Desk 3, brings 2150's paperwork to Lu. Every official must now pass an exam.

rules.name: Sun Tzu's art of business
rules.news: THE ART OF WAR, VOLUME TWO: Sun Tzu, stamped home at Desk 3, writes a strategy for 2150. Every merchant in Lu buys a copy.

rules.name: The First Emperor standardises 2150
rules.news: ONE STANDARD FOR ALL: Qin Shi Huang, stamped home at Desk 3, makes 2150's forms the law of China. All axles match.

rules.name: Caesar's new calendar
rules.news: VENI, VIDI, VICI: Julius Caesar, stamped home at Desk 3, gives Rome 2150's calendar. Nobody can find the Ides of March.

rules.name: Archimedes moves the Earth
rules.news: EUREKA: Archimedes, stamped home at Desk 3, builds 2150's reactor with a lever and a mirror. Syracuse glows at night.

rules.name: Marco Polo's paper money
rules.news: IT IS ALL TRUE: Marco Polo, stamped home at Desk 3, tells Venice about 2150. This time the Rialto believes him.

rules.name: Genghis Khan's relay
rules.news: THE GREAT RELAY: Genghis Khan, stamped home at Desk 3, wires 2150's network into his post riders. A message crosses Asia in a day.

rules.name: Galileo's telescope
rules.news: AND YET IT MOVES: Galileo Galilei, stamped home at Desk 3, points 2150's telescope at the sky. Padua sees the rings of Saturn.

rules.name: Nobunaga's free markets
rules.news: FREE MARKETS, FREE GUILDS: Oda Nobunaga, stamped home at Desk 3, opens Azuchi to 2150's trade. Every castle town booms.

rules.name: Hokusai's great wave
rules.news: THE GREAT WAVE OF 2150: Katsushika Hokusai, stamped home at Desk 3, prints 2150 rising behind Mount Fuji. Every house in Edo buys one.

rules.name: Elizabeth's company
rules.news: THE GOLDEN AGE, CHARTERED: Elizabeth I, stamped home at Desk 3, charters a company for 2150's trade. London becomes a boardroom.

rules.name: Newton's laws of credit
rules.news: EVERY ACTION, AN EQUAL REACTION: Isaac Newton, stamped home at Desk 3, runs the Royal Mint on 2150's credit. London's coins never wear down.

rules.name: Luther's door
rules.news: 95 THESES ON 2150: Martin Luther, stamped home at Desk 3, nails 2150's ideas to a church door. Every German reads them in print.

rules.name: Beethoven's ninth
rules.news: ODE TO JOY: Ludwig van Beethoven, stamped home at Desk 3, writes a symphony for 2150. All men become brothers by the fourth movement.

rules.name: Marx reads 2150's accounts
rules.news: WORKERS OF ALL TIMES: Karl Marx, stamped home at Desk 3, writes a book about 2150's debts. Cologne's workers form a council.

rules.name: Hammurabi's new law
rules.news: DEBTS FORGIVEN: Hammurabi, stamped home at Desk 3, carves a law from 2150 into stone. Babylon cancels every debt.

rules.name: Michelangelo's ceiling
rules.news: A CEILING FOR 2150: Michelangelo, stamped home at Desk 3, paints the future on a chapel ceiling. Pilgrims queue for a look.

rules.name: Kurosawa films the future
rules.news: THE FUTURE IN COLOUR: Akira Kurosawa, stamped home at Desk 3, films 2150 in Tokyo. Every queue is an epic now.

rules.name: Shakespeare's play about 2150
rules.news: ALL THE WORLD'S A STAGE: William Shakespeare, stamped home at Desk 3, writes a play about 2150. London queues round the Globe.

rules.name: Darwin's green London
rules.news: ORIGIN OF THE FUTURE: Charles Darwin, stamped home at Desk 3, tells London what 2150 evolved into. Gardens grow on every roof.

rules.name: Einstein's atomic Berlin
rules.news: E=MC2 FOR ALL: Albert Einstein, stamped home at Desk 3, brings 2150's physics to Berlin. Atomic kettles go on sale.

outcomes.name: The Directorate
outcomes.headline: DIRECTORATE: the Customs Directorate carries on running 2150. The queues reopen at nine, as always.
outcomes.report: The Customs Directorate runs 2150 as it always has: by form, by queue and by stamp. Every citizen knows exactly which counter to stand at.

outcomes.name: Democracy
outcomes.headline: 2150 VOTES: the Directorate hands the building to an elected assembly. Its first sitting ran eleven hours.
outcomes.report: An elected assembly runs 2150 and votes on everything, including the colour of the ballot papers. Anyone may stand for office, and nearly everyone does.

outcomes.name: Monarchy
outcomes.headline: A CROWN FOR 2150: a monarch is proclaimed on the Directorate steps. The queues are now royal queues.
outcomes.report: A monarch reigns over 2150 from a palace that used to be a transit hall. Every form carries the royal crest, and people have started framing them.

outcomes.name: Fascism
outcomes.headline: ORDER: a single party takes charge of 2150. Uniforms are issued, and every portal opens to the second.
outcomes.report: One party runs 2150, and one flag hangs over every portal. The timetables are exact, the parades are long, and nobody steps out of the queue.

outcomes.name: Communism
outcomes.headline: THE PEOPLE'S DESK: workers' councils take over the Directorate. Every desk now has a committee.
outcomes.report: Workers' councils run 2150 and hold the portals in common. Every clerk is a comrade, every queue is shared equally, and the five-year plan has a ten-year appendix.

outcomes.name: Theocracy
outcomes.headline: BY SACRED ORDER: 2150's temple councils take up the Directorate's duties. The stamps are blessed each morning.
outcomes.report: Temple councils govern 2150, and every departure begins with a blessing of the portal. The calendar has many more holidays, and the queues wait in respectful silence.

outcomes.name: Technocracy
outcomes.headline: RUN BY EXPERTS: a council of engineers takes over 2150. Its first decree is a flowchart.
outcomes.report: Engineers and statisticians run 2150 through committees of specialists. Every law comes with footnotes, and every citizen with a user manual.

outcomes.name: The Corporate Board
outcomes.headline: UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT: a board of directors acquires 2150. Every citizen receives a shareholder newsletter.
outcomes.report: A corporate board runs 2150 as a going concern, with quarterly meetings open to anyone holding a share. The minutes are glossy, and the annual report has a mascot.

outcomes.name: The Credit Age
outcomes.headline: THE CREDIT AGE: wrist comms, queues and the debt grid carry on. 2150 runs on credit, as before.
outcomes.report: 2150 runs on wrist comms, credit lines and very long queues. Everything is on account, and the account is always open.

outcomes.name: The Nuclear Age
outcomes.headline: ATOMS FOR ALL: 2150's first home reactor goes on sale. Kettles now boil in a second.
outcomes.report: 2150 runs on the atom: reactors in the basements and a gentle glow on the night shift. Power is too cheap to meter, so nobody meters it.

outcomes.name: The Cybernetic Age
outcomes.headline: WIRED: 2150 connects its citizens straight to the city grid. Queue numbers now arrive by thought.
outcomes.report: 2150 runs on implants and thinking machines. Its citizens talk to the city, and the city answers back, usually politely.

outcomes.name: The Space Age
outcomes.headline: LIFT-OFF: the first launch ring opens over the Aegean. The Space League is hiring.
outcomes.report: 2150 looks up: launch rings, orbital suburbs and a weekend commute to the Moon. The luggage limits are strict; the view is spectacular.

outcomes.name: Naturalism
outcomes.headline: BACK TO THE LAND: 2150 switched off the grid for a week, and nobody switched it back on. Vineyards climb the arcologies.
outcomes.report: 2150 has rewilded itself: gardens in the transit halls, goats on the portals and meetings held under trees. Everything grows, and the paperwork is composted.

outcomes.name: Anarchy
outcomes.headline: NOBODY'S PLAN: 2150's master plans are cancelled by general agreement. Every street now runs itself.
outcomes.report: 2150 runs on whatever works that day: self-built districts, street assemblies and improvised machines. There is no timetable, and yet things arrive.

outcomes.name: The Debt
outcomes.headline: THE DEBT HOLDS: every account in 2150 carries over. Interest compounds as usual.
outcomes.report: 2150 pays its way on credit: every citizen carries a debt, and every debt passes to kin. The ledger has never once lost track of a cent.

outcomes.name: Jubilee
outcomes.headline: JUBILEE: every debt in 2150 is forgiven at midnight. Collections throws a party.
outcomes.report: Every debt in 2150 was forgiven, and the ledgers were shredded into confetti. Nobody owes anybody, and the collectors are learning to knit.

outcomes.name: Company Towns
outcomes.headline: COMPANY TOWN: 2150's employers take over housing, schools and the portals. Wages are paid in company scrip.
outcomes.report: 2150's employers run daily life: company housing, company schools, company songs. Payday comes in scrip, and the canteen is very popular.

outcomes.name: The Commons
outcomes.headline: SHARE AND SHARE ALIKE: everything in 2150 goes into common stores. The first swap market opens in the transit hall.
outcomes.report: 2150 shares what it has: common stores, swap markets and a library of tools. Nothing is bought; everything is borrowed and, mostly, returned.

outcomes.name: The Banking Houses
outcomes.headline: HOUSES OF CREDIT: the merchant dynasties open their vaults to 2150. Every family now has a banker.
outcomes.report: Merchant banking dynasties finance 2150 from marble halls, lending by letter and by handshake. The interest is negotiable, and lunch is included.
